title: Emails in Marketing
subtitle: Simple language for writing and responding to professional marketing emails
description: Email is one of the most common tools in B2B marketing. In this lesson, you will learn the basic words and phrases you need to write clear, professional marketing emails — from the opening greeting to the sign-off.
dialogueSubtitle: Dana asks Riley for help writing a marketing email to a potential client

questions: Do you write emails in English at work? What kinds of things do you write about?
What is the difference between a formal email and an informal email? Can you give an example?
Have you ever received a marketing email that made you want to find out more? What did it say?

vocabulary.definition: The title of an email that the reader sees before they open it. A good subject line makes people want to open the email.
vocabulary.example: Riley spent ten minutes on the subject line because she knew it would decide whether the client opens the email or deletes it.

vocabulary.definition: The first line of an email where you say hello to the reader. For example: 'Dear Mr Brown' or 'Hi Sarah'.
vocabulary.example: Dana used 'Dear' as her greeting because she had never met the client before and wanted to be formal.

vocabulary.definition: The first paragraph of an email where you say who you are and why you are writing.
vocabulary.example: Keep your introduction short — say who you are and your reason for writing in two or three sentences.

vocabulary.definition: To add a file — like a document, PDF, or image — to an email so the reader can download it.
vocabulary.example: I will attach our brochure to the email so the client can read more about our services.

vocabulary.definition: To send a response to an email that someone sent you.
vocabulary.example: The client did not reply to our first email, so Riley sent a short follow-up message the next week.

vocabulary.definition: A sentence near the end of an email that tells the reader what to do next — for example: 'Book a free call' or 'Reply to this email'.
vocabulary.example: Every marketing email needs a clear call to action — without it, the reader does not know what step to take.

vocabulary.definition: The closing words at the end of an email before your name. For example: 'Best regards' or 'Kind regards'.
vocabulary.example: Riley used 'Best regards' as her sign-off because it sounds professional but not too formal.

vocabulary.definition: A second email or message you send after the first one, usually because the person did not reply.
vocabulary.example: If the client does not reply in five days, send a follow-up — keep it short and friendly.

phrasalVerbs.definition: To contact someone — usually by email or phone — to start a conversation or offer help.
phrasalVerbs.example: I am reaching out to introduce our agency and see if we can help with your marketing.

phrasalVerbs.definition: To contact someone again after an earlier message or meeting, usually to get a response.
phrasalVerbs.example: If you do not hear back in a week, follow up with a short email — remind them who you are.

phrasalVerbs.definition: To reply to someone after a delay — often used when someone has been waiting for an answer.
phrasalVerbs.example: Thank you for your email — I will get back to you by the end of the week with more details.

phrasalVerbs.definition: To feel positive about something that is going to happen. Used in formal emails to end on a polite note.
phrasalVerbs.example: I look forward to hearing from you and hope we can arrange a call next week.

phrasalVerbs.definition: To add a document or file to an email before you send it.
phrasalVerbs.example: I have attached our company brochure to this email — please take a look when you have a moment.

phrasalVerbs.definition: To reply to a message. More informal than 'reply' — used in less formal email conversations.
phrasalVerbs.example: Please write back if you have any questions about the proposal — I am happy to explain more.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Riley, I need to write a marketing email to a new company. I do not know them yet. How should I start?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Start with the [[subject line:the title of an email that the reader sees before they open it]]. It is the most important part — if it is not interesting, they will not open the email.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: What makes a good subject line?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Keep it short — under ten words. Make it clear and useful. For example: 'How we helped a B2B company get 30% more leads'.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Okay. And what about the [[greeting:the first line of an email where you say hello]]? Should I write 'Dear' or 'Hi'?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: If you do not know them, use 'Dear' — it is more formal. Then use their first name: 'Dear Sarah' — not 'Dear Sir or Madam'.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Good. Then I write my [[introduction:the first paragraph where you say who you are and why you are writing]]?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Yes — two or three sentences. Say who you are, how you found them, and why you are writing. Keep it short.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Should I [[attach:to add a file to an email]] the brochure?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Yes, attach the brochure. But do not make the email too long. End with a clear [[call to action:a sentence that tells the reader what to do next]] — like 'Would you like to book a quick call?'

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: And if they do not [[reply:to send a response to an email]]?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Send a [[follow-up:a second email sent after the first one]] after five days. Keep it very short — just two or three lines. Use a friendly [[sign-off:the closing words at the end of an email before your name]] like 'Best regards'.

The attachment — people always open files.

completeSentenceExercise.instructions: Choose the correct word or phrase to complete each sentence. Then read the sentence aloud.

items.sentence: Keep your _____ short — under ten words — so it is easy to read in a busy inbox.
options: subject line
greeting
sign-off
items.explanation: Subject line is the title of the email — the part people see before they open it. Greeting is the hello at the start. Sign-off is the ending. The subject line must be short and interesting because it decides if someone opens the email.

items.sentence: I will _____ our company brochure to this email — please take a look when you have a moment.
options: reply
attach
follow up
items.explanation: Attach means to add a file to an email. Reply means to send a response. Follow up means to contact someone again after an earlier message. Attach is correct — you are adding a file (the brochure) to the email.

items.sentence: Every good marketing email needs a clear _____ — the reader must know what to do next.
options: greeting
follow-up
call to action
items.explanation: Call to action is a sentence that tells the reader what to do next. Greeting is how you say hello. Follow-up is a second email. The call to action is what turns a good email into one that gets results.

items.sentence: If the client does not reply in five days, send a short _____ to remind them of your email.
options: subject line
follow-up
introduction
items.explanation: Follow-up is a second email sent because the first one did not get a reply. Subject line is the title of the email. Introduction is the opening paragraph. Always follow up — most clients need a second message before they reply.

items.sentence: I am _____ to your email about the proposal — I have some questions for you.
options: attaching
replying
reaching out
items.explanation: Replying means sending a response to an email. Attaching means adding a file. Reaching out means making first contact. Replying is correct because you are responding to an email you received.

items.sentence: Dana used 'Best regards' as her _____ — it sounds professional but not too formal.
options: sign-off
greeting
call to action
items.explanation: Sign-off is the closing phrase before your name — like 'Best regards' or 'Kind regards'. Greeting is the opening hello. Call to action is the instruction at the end. The sign-off leaves a final professional impression.

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in pairs. Read each situation and choose the best response. Talk about why before you click.

items.customerLine: A potential client replies to your email: 'Thanks for reaching out. What services do you offer exactly?'
options: Reply with your full price list and all 12 services you offer — give them everything they need to decide.
Reply with a short summary of your two or three most relevant services for their industry, and suggest a quick call to find out more about their needs.
Wait two days before replying so you look professional and not too eager.
items.explanation: B is correct. Sending too much information at once can overwhelm the client. A short, relevant summary plus a call suggestion keeps the conversation going. A sends too much information. C — waiting two days will make you look unresponsive, not professional.

items.customerLine: You sent a marketing email one week ago and heard nothing. What do you do?
options: Do nothing — if they were interested, they would have replied.
Send a follow-up email. Keep it very short — two or three lines. Say who you are, remind them of your first email, and ask if they had a chance to read it.
Call them and ask why they did not reply to your email.
items.explanation: B is correct. A short, polite follow-up is standard practice in B2B marketing. Most clients need two or three touches before they reply. A gives up too early. C — calling to ask why they did not reply is too aggressive and will make a bad first impression.

items.customerLine: A new client asks: 'Is there anything you can send me to learn more about your agency?'
options: Say: Our website has all the information — just go to www.example.com.
Say: Of course — I will attach our company brochure and a case study that is relevant to your industry. Let me know if you have any questions after reading.
Say: I will send you our full proposal with pricing. I will need three to four days to prepare it.
items.explanation: B is correct. Attaching a brochure and a relevant case study gives the client what they asked for in a useful, personalised way. A sends them away from the conversation — you lose the personal connection. C jumps to a full proposal before you understand their needs.

spotTheMistake.instructions: Read this marketing email. There are 3 mistakes. Find them and correct them. Work in pairs.

dialogue.speaker: Body
dialogue.text: I am writing to introduce our agency, MarketBridge. We help B2B companies grow their marketing and generate more leads.

dialogue.speaker: Body
dialogue.text: I have attach our brochure to this email. Please take a look when you have a moment.

dialogue.speaker: Body
dialogue.text: If you are interested, please let us know.

mistakes.correction: How we helped a B2B company get 30% more leads
mistakes.explanation: The subject line 'Our marketing services' is too generic — it tells the reader nothing interesting. A strong subject line gives a specific benefit or result. For example: 'How we helped a B2B company get 30% more leads'. This makes the reader want to open the email.

'To whom it may concern' is very old-fashioned and impersonal. In modern B2B email, always use the person's first name if you have it — for example: 'Dear Sarah,' or 'Hi Sarah,'. It makes the email feel personal and shows you did your research.

'I have attach' is a grammar mistake. The correct form is 'I have attached' — this uses the present perfect tense (have + past participle). The past participle of 'attach' is 'attached', not 'attach'.

finishTheLine.instructions: Finish the salesperson's line. Use language from this lesson. Then compare with a partner.

items.customerLine: Client: Your email looks interesting. Can you tell me a bit more about what you do?
items.salespersonStart: Of course — I would be happy to. We help B2B companies
items.suggestedCompletion: grow their marketing, generate leads, and reach the right audience. I have attached a short brochure to this email with more details. Would it be useful to arrange a 20-minute call this week? I can answer any questions you have and learn more about your goals.

items.customerLine: Client: I received your email but I have been very busy. Can you send it again?
items.salespersonStart: No problem at all — I completely understand.
items.suggestedCompletion: I have attached the brochure again below. The key thing I wanted to share is how we helped a company in your industry increase their leads by 30% in three months. Would you be open to a quick call next week to talk about whether we could do something similar for you?

items.customerLine: Client: We are not sure if we need a marketing agency right now.
items.salespersonStart: I understand — it is a big decision.
items.suggestedCompletion: There is no pressure at all. I would love to have a short call just to learn more about your goals. Sometimes after one conversation, people realise where the gaps are — and sometimes they decide they do not need us yet. Either way, it is a useful 20 minutes. Would that work for you?
